messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Phommasack is a thirty-four-year-old Lao-American chaplain, widowed two years ago after the illness and death of his wife, who came to clinical attention following a street robbery that occurred approximately seven months before his intake appointment. He presented with a PCL-5 score of 77, indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and described a presentation that had quietly dismantled much of the spiritual equanimity he had spent years cultivating.

The robbery took place on a Tuesday evening as Kiet was walking back from a hospital visit to a parishioner. A man approached him rapidly from behind on a narrow sidewalk, pressed close enough that Kiet could hear the ragged, laboured sound of his breathing — the hot, irregular rhythm of it — before demanding his wallet and phone. A second man appeared from a doorway to Kiet's left, boxing him in. The physical crowding was total and suffocating; Kiet recalls the smell of cigarette smoke and something chemical, like cleaning solvent, mixing with the night air. He handed over what he had. The men were gone within seconds. He stood alone on the pavement for a long time before he could move.

In the months that followed, Kiet found that certain things returned him to that sidewalk with an immediacy that felt less like remembering and more like re-entering. The memories themselves arrived primarily as images — the dark shape of the man's arm, the angle of the doorway, the particular quality of the streetlight — vivid and arrested, like photographs he could not put down. Alongside the visual fragments came smell: that specific compound of smoke and solvent would surface without warning, and with it the whole scene reconstituted itself. When these memories broke through, they were not accompanied by fear alone. What Kiet reported most forcefully was rage — an intense, disorienting fury that felt alien to him given his vocation and that he had no framework for managing.

These sensory memories were reliably ignited by a specific cluster of situations. Crowded places — the hospital corridors where Kiet worked, the packed waiting rooms he moved through daily as part of his pastoral rounds — compressed him in ways that made the images surge forward. The sound of heavy breathing, whether from an elderly patient, a crying family member, or simply someone exerting themselves nearby, functioned as an almost mechanical key, unlocking the auditory texture of that night and flooding him with the images and the rage that accompanied them. Even encountering people he associated with the event — a colleague who had been on the ward that evening, the neighbourhood near the hospital — was sufficient to pull the memories to the surface. In this way, the triggers did not merely remind Kiet of what had happened; they reinstated it.

What made the clinical picture more complex, and more painful, was what Kiet had concluded about himself in the wake of the robbery. He had come to believe, with a quiet but corrosive certainty, that the event had happened because of the kind of person he was — that something in his character, his carelessness, his passivity, had made him a target. He was certain that another man, someone more capable or more alert, would simply not have found himself in that situation. Most damaging of all was his conviction that he was constitutionally unable to prevent bad things from happening to him — that his wife's death and now this were not coincidences but evidence of a pattern rooted in who he was. These appraisals fed directly back into the memories, colouring them with shame and self-contempt that deepened the rage he felt on recall. They also amplified his sensitivity to the triggers themselves: because he understood crowded spaces and certain people as environments in which his inadequacy would again be exposed, his vigilance in those settings was absolute, and the threshold for memory intrusion dropped accordingly.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a pastoral visit in which a patient's laboured breathing caused him to leave the room abruptly and stand in the corridor, shaking, for several minutes — unable to return, unable to explain himself. He had begun to fear he could no longer do his work. What he hoped for, he said carefully, was not to stop remembering, but to stop feeling that the memory proved something true about him.
